results.summary_before: This analog block implements the fine-resolution part of a time-to-digital converter using time interpolation. It converts an input pulse of 20 to 60 nanoseconds into a periodic square wave with a period 90 times longer, allowing a low-frequency counter to measure the pulse width with high resolution. The circuit requires external hardware including a signal generator, a 13uA current source, and an oscilloscope for testing. It is a transistor-level analog design intended for applications such as digital communications, radar, and particle physics.

Testing requires a typical experimental PLL or VCO bench setup, and no digital control pins are provided. The design is notable as a transistor-level analog exploration of PLL building blocks on a shared shuttle.

results.summary_before: This project implements a Serializer and Deserializer (SerDes) module that converts 8-bit parallel data to a 10-bit encoded serial stream and back. It uses 8b/10b encoding for data integrity and includes control signals for enabling serialization, deserialization, and data latching. The design is purely digital and requires no external hardware, making it suitable for integration into larger systems. The documentation is thorough but lacks silicon test results.

It includes data, serial, parallel, and serialization enable control signals plus a synchronous reset, with latch and shift-register elements synchronizing the paths. The design is purely digital and requires no external hardware, making it suitable for integration into larger systems. The documentation is thorough but contains no silicon test results.

results.summary_before: This is a video and audio player that reads binary 80x60 pixel video and PCM/PWM audio data from an external SPI NOR flash chip and outputs it as 640x480 VGA with audio. It supports configurable audio type (PCM or PWM), VGA PMOD type, and pixel colors via input pins. External hardware includes a VGA monitor, a Tiny VGA PMOD, an SPI flash chip (W25Q128JVSSIQ), and for PWM audio an external DAC. The design is notable for playing the 'Bad Apple' video and demonstrating complex data streaming from flash.

results.summary_before: This analog design uses a Twin Tee notch filter with an opamp to generate a sine wave at approximately 4.93 MHz. A 20-bit digital counter is connected to the oscillator output, with the top 8 bits driving the LEDs, so the most significant bit flashes about 5 times per second. An oscilloscope is required to observe the sine wave, and the design is sensitive to loading, so it should be started with no scope connected. Silicon testing by the author shows it oscillates at about 4.6 MHz and the counter works, though the sine wave quality is moderate.
